transcript.text: I am the business intelligence analyst at a retailer that sells in its own shops and online across the UAE. The chief executive wants one weekly revenue dashboard, by region, channel and product category, that everyone trusts. Last month the sales director reported revenue about nine percent higher than finance did for the same weeks, and each says the other is wrong. Both teams start from the export I shared: one row per order with an order id, the order date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer id. The status column shows how each order ended. I would like the dashboard built from this table so I can present it at Monday's management meeting. The chief executive will use it to judge the regional managers. [shares sales.csv]

[DCLab drew a dashboard above this message]

Here's what I found and what I built. Monthly, the same split: January 2026 **32,186.50** booked against **26,931.85** paid only, February **26,344.62** against **23,294.03**, March **26,122.16** against **22,456.18**. Neither team is wrong; one is reporting booked demand, the other collected revenue. **The dashboard is shown** (6 tiles, refreshable): weekly booked vs net collected vs refunded vs cancelled for 2026 to date; weekly net revenue by region and by channel; revenue by product category split across the three statuses; refund and cancellation share by region; and monthly booked vs net across the whole file. Headline is net collected (paid only), with booked and the two leakages always visible beside it, so sales and finance see their own number in the same picture. **Two things to settle before Monday.** Dubai is the biggest region on both counts — **167,813.71** net and **19,300.08** refunded — so how refunds are treated moves it most; Ajman's **35,619.49** net has no cancellations recorded at all, which is worth a sanity check.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

transcript.text: I am the commercial director of a building-materials distributor. Last year we bought a competitor, so we now have two customer lists: about 4,000 accounts in our system and 2,500 in theirs. I want a customer lifetime value model on the combined list so we know which accounts deserve a key-account manager; we can afford one for about 150 accounts. Each system has its own account numbers. Company names were typed by hand, the same contractor often has a separate account for each building site or branch, and many firms bought from both of us. Both systems hold three years of invoices with the account number, date and amount. Nothing is exported yet. My sales reps say the big customers are obvious and the list should find the ones they miss.

What I hear you asking for isn't really a lifetime-value model — it's a decision about 150 scarce people. And the thing most likely to wreck that decision is that your two lists aren't lists of customers, they're lists of accounts. With one contractor holding a separate account per site or branch, and many firms buying from both of you before the deal, a value ranking run at account level would fill your key-account slots with branches of the same few big names, and bury the mid-sized firm whose spend is split across two systems. That's precisely the "ones the reps miss". So the merge comes first, whatever we build after it.

My plan:

1. Export both systems — 3 years of invoices plus one row per account with whatever identifies the firm behind it. Checked by row counts and totals against what each system reports, so nothing is dropped in transit.
2. Build the customer master: exact matches where a registration/VAT number or billing postcode agrees, fuzzy name-and-address matches for the rest, and a short review file of borderline pairs your team rules on. Stop only if merges can't be made confidently; those firms stay separate and get flagged.
3. Score every firm on combined spend, order frequency, recency and 3-year trend — one score per firm, not per account.
4. Produce the ranked shortlist to 150 with the reason each firm is there, and a separate "look here" list: small per account, large once merged.
5. If you want more than history, add a forward model, back-tested by training on the first two years and checking it against the third.

One thing to say plainly: you described amount only, so this ranks revenue. If your export can carry cost or margin, the list changes — key accounts you lose money on are worth catching.

Three ways to start are below. And one question: when you export an account, what fields come with it besides the number — a VAT or company registration number, billing address or postcode?

choices.what: Take a 3-year invoice export from each system, normalise the hand-typed names, and resolve accounts into real firms: exact matches first (registration/VAT number or billing postcode), then fuzzy name-and-address matches, with the borderline ones left in a short review file for your team to sign off. You get: One row per firm, carrying its accounts from both systems and its combined history - the file every later answer is built on. Trade-off: No ranking yet, and someone has to rule on the uncertain merges. Effort: Quick to run; the review is the only human work.

choices.title: Rank the firms and pick the 150
choices.what: Run the merge above, then score each firm on combined spend, order frequency, recency and 3-year trend, and rank at firm level rather than account level. You get: A shortlist of key-account candidates with the reason each one is there, plus a flag for firms that look small per account but are large once merged - the ones your reps say get missed. Trade-off: Backward-looking: it ranks what they have already spent, on revenue unless you can export margin. Effort: The merge plus one scoring pass; results in this chat.

choices.what: You get: A ranked list that includes firms not big yet but rising, and a defensible cut line at 150. Trade-off: Most set-up, and it needs the merge to be solid before the numbers mean anything. Effort: A project rather than a one-off answer.

transcript.text: Merged customer master first

Started: the merged customer master, as a data-preparation project. Here's what happens in order.

**Step 1 — you export four files**, one pair per system. Per system:

- *Account master*, one row per account: account number, name exactly as typed, trading name if separate, VAT or company registration number, billing address and postcode, delivery addresses, phone, main contact, customer-since date, and which rep or branch owns it.
- *Invoices*, one row per invoice: account number, invoice date, invoice number, amount — and net value and cost or margin if the system carries them. Include credit notes as negative rows, don't strip them.

CSV or Excel, whichever your IT person prefers. Nothing needs tidying first; hand-typed names are the problem I expect to solve, not something I want pre-cleaned.

**Step 2 — I check the files load whole.** Row counts and invoice totals per system reconciled against what each system reports, so we never build on a partial export.

**Step 3 — I build the customer master.** Confident matches first where a registration number or billing postcode agrees; then name-and-address similarity for the rest; then a short review file of borderline pairs for your team to rule on. Firms that can't be matched confidently stay split and get flagged rather than guessed.

**Step 4 — the deliverable:** one row per *firm*, with how many accounts it spans in each system, combined 3-year spend, and a confidence marker on each merge.

The one thing I need from you: of those identity fields, which ones actually exist in your systems? Registration or VAT number is worth more than anything else on that list — if it's held, the merge becomes reliable rather than best-effort.
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

Then these are my calls, locked in so we don't relitigate them when the files land. **Grain.** Everything downstream is scored per *firm*, never per account. An account is what your systems hold; a firm is what deserves a key-account manager. **Matching, in this order.** Registration or VAT number where it exists — the only match I'd trust blind. Then billing postcode or full address combined with name similarity. Then whatever is left that looks like a pair goes into a review file for your team, capped at a few hundred pairs so it's an afternoon's work, not a project. Everything else stays split and gets flagged. I will not guess a merge to make the list look tidy; a wrong merge inflates one firm and erases another, which is worse than an honest split. **Value.** Revenue from invoiced amount, unless the export can carry cost or margin. If it can, send it — a key-account list built on revenue alone will hand a manager to firms that buy the lowest-margin product lines. Credit notes come as negative rows; don't strip them, they're how returns and rebates stay visible. **The export, four files:** for each system — *account master*, one row per account (account number, name as typed, trading name, VAT/registration number, billing address and postcode, delivery addresses, phone, main contact, customer-since date, owning branch or rep); and *invoices*, one row per invoice (account number, invoice date, invoice number, amount, plus net value or cost if held). Raw CSV, nothing tidied beforehand. Hand-typed names are the thing I'm solving, not something to pre-clean. Send those four files here when you have them — I'll reconcile row counts and invoice totals against each system before touching a single match. If it helps, I can draft the export request as a message you can forward to IT.

transcript.text: I am the revenue manager of a travel agency that sells in the UAE and, since last year, to customers in Europe through our website. Cancellations cost us a lot, so I plan to ask for a non-refundable deposit from the bookings most likely to be cancelled and keep the normal terms for everyone else. Please build the model that decides who must pay the deposit. The table I shared has one row per booking: booking date, travel date, destination, the customer's nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether free cancellation was offered, and whether the booking was cancelled. From what I have seen in our reports, nationality tells the most about who cancels, so I expect it to be the main input. The website would apply the rule automatically at checkout. [shares bookings.csv]

Nationality looks flatter than your reports suggest — let me check where the real signal sits before building.

Understood: you want a rule that ranks each new booking by cancellation risk at checkout, so only the top-risk ones are asked for a non-refundable deposit, and the website applies it automatically. I've started the build on that basis. One thing in your data is worth knowing before I train, because it changes what you'll ask the model to do. Nationality barely moves the odds: GB 27.8%, IN 21.6%, SA 21.2%, AE 21.9%, PK 23.7%, IR 21.0% — all around your overall rate of 22.9% (343 cancellations in 1,500 bookings). Channel is equally flat (agent 23.8%, web 22.6%, app 22.6%), and the free-cancellation flag hardly matters (22.6% without vs 23.3% with). What does separate is lead time: bookings that were cancelled had a median of 109 days to travel, against 87 days for those kept, and destination ranges from Paris 18.9% to Dubai 26.2%. So a deposit rule keyed mainly on nationality would be sorting your European customers on a weak signal — and it's the kind of rule that invites complaints in the EU. I'd rather let lead time and price do the work, and I'll train it twice, with and without nationality, so you can see the difference for yourself. The plan: clean price (stored as text, not numbers) and drop the 12 'TEST' destination rows; train on bookings and validate only on later ones, never a random mix; report the cut-off's catch rate against the 22.9% baseline; compare with/without nationality; then set the score line that asks the fewest deposits for the most cancellations caught. Two data notes: the table can't tell me whether a customer walks away when asked for a deposit, so that risk needs a small test launch. And to place the cut-off properly, what does one cancellation cost you, and what deposit would you charge?

Last month the sales director reported revenue about nine percent higher than finance did for the same weeks, and each says the other is wrong. What you need is not a predictive model first. You need a single, agreed revenue rule that can be applied to the order file and then audited.

## What the problem is

The real decision is this: **which order-level records count as revenue, for which week, and in which unit**, so the chief executive can compare regions and managers on the same basis.

The users are:

- the chief executive, who wants one weekly revenue dashboard;
- the sales director, who needs the number to reflect what the sales team sold or invoiced;
- finance, who needs the number to reflect recognized, collected, or booked revenue;
- regional managers, who will be judged by the regional view;
- you, as the business intelligence analyst, who has to make the result trustworthy and repeatable.

The unit is money: an amount for each order, aggregated into weekly totals.

The moment is the week in which revenue is recognized. That is likely where the conflict comes from. One team may be counting the order when it was placed, another when it was completed, delivered, invoiced, collected, refunded, or posted in finance.

What you have told me:

- the dashboard must be weekly;
- it must break down by region, channel, and product category;
- it must cover both shops and online sales across the UAE;
- the source is one row per order;
- the file has these fields: `order_id`, `order_date`, `region`, `channel`, `product_category`, `amount`, `status`, `customer_id`;
- both sales and finance start from the same export;
- last month the sales number was about nine percent higher than finance for the same weeks;
- each side believes the other is wrong;
- the dashboard is needed for Monday’s management meeting.

What I do not know:

- what each value in `status` means;
- whether `amount` includes VAT, discounts, shipping, returns, refunds, or adjustments;
- whether finance uses a different revenue recognition date;
- whether “revenue” means gross ordered value, net completed value, invoiced value, collected value, or booked revenue;
- whether cancelled or returned orders should be removed, offset, or shown separately;
- whether there are duplicate orders, amended orders, or late status updates;
- whether region is sales team region, shop region, delivery region, customer region, or finance cost-center region;
- whether the week starts Monday or Sunday;
- whether the `order_date` is enough for finance reporting or whether a delivery, invoice, or payment date is needed.

Because of this, the safest answer is: **make the definition explicit, then build the dashboard from that definition and reconcile it against finance and sales.**

## Approaches that could solve it

### 1. No model at all: simple aggregation with a single agreed definition

This means choosing one rule, for example:

> Weekly net recognized revenue = the sum of `amount` for orders whose status belongs to a finance-approved recognized-revenue set, grouped by ISO week, region, channel, and product category.

Cost:

- low technical cost;
- medium political and governance cost, because sales, finance, and leadership must agree on the rule.

What it gives:

- one number for the dashboard;
- a clear rule people can check;
- a path to trust, if the definition is signed off.

Risk:

- if finance and sales do not agree, the dashboard will still be disputed.

### 2. Build several clearly labelled revenue views

For example:

- gross ordered revenue;
- net completed revenue;
- finance-recognized revenue;
- excluded cancellations and refunds.

Cost:

- more reporting time;
- more explanation for the chief executive.

What it gives:

- transparency;
- a way to show why sales and finance differ.

Risk:

- it may not meet the request for “one trusted dashboard.” It can become “three numbers” unless the primary metric is clearly chosen.

### 3. Build a reconciliation layer before the dashboard

This means comparing the export-based revenue to finance’s revenue and showing exactly where the difference comes from: status, duplicates, tax, returns, timing, missing data, or definition.

Cost:

- more work before Monday;
- requires finance cooperation;
- requires row-level checks.

What it gives:

- the strongest basis for trust;
- an audit trail;
- a defensible answer if the chief executive asks why regional managers are being judged differently.

Risk:

- if the export does not contain finance’s recognition date, the reconciliation may only approximate the difference.

### 4. Apply machine learning or forecasting

This would be a wrong approach here.

Cost:

- high effort;
- unclear benefit;
- it does not resolve the disagreement about what revenue means.

What it gives:

- maybe a forecast of future revenue;
- not the trusted current-week revenue dashboard needed for Monday.

I would not use this approach.

## My recommended approach

Use **Approach 1 plus the reconciliation discipline from Approach 3**:

> Build one weekly net revenue dashboard using a single, written revenue definition, and validate it with a reconciliation waterfall so every difference from the raw export to the dashboard is explained.

This is the only approach likely to satisfy both the chief executive’s need for one number and the practical need to resolve the sales-versus-finance dispute.

## The plan

### Step 1: Agree the revenue definition before building

You need a short written definition, ideally approved by finance and the sales director before Monday.

The definition must say:

1. **Which orders count as revenue**
   - Include or exclude based on `status`.
   - State whether completed, shipped, paid, delivered, returned, cancelled, refunded, or pending orders are recognized.

2. **Which amount counts**
   - Whether `amount` is gross sale value, net sale value, or finance-recognized value.
   - Whether VAT, discounts, shipping, returns, and adjustments are included or excluded.

3. **Which date defines the week**
   - Whether the dashboard uses `order_date` because that is what is available, or whether finance’s recognition date is required.
   - If only `order_date` is available, say clearly that weekly revenue is based on order date and status, not necessarily finance posting date.

4. **Which region is used**
   - Whether `region` means the selling region, the shop location, the delivery region, the customer region, or the finance reporting region.

5. **How returns and cancellations are treated**
   - Are they removed from revenue?
   - Are they recorded as negative revenue?
   - Are they shown separately?

6. **How duplicate or amended orders are treated**
   - Is `order_id` unique?
   - Are revised orders replaced or added?

You can ask for approval in a short meeting or email. For Monday, the important thing is to state the rule clearly and have finance and sales either agree or identify the exact exception.

### Step 2: Check the data quality of the export

Before aggregating, verify:

1. `order_id`
   - Are there duplicate order IDs?
   - Do duplicate order IDs have different amounts, statuses, dates, regions, or customers?

2. `order_date`
   - Are there missing dates?
   - Are dates outside the expected week or year?
   - Do they fall in the correct timezone?

3. `amount`
   - Are there missing amounts?
   - Are there negative amounts?
   - Do negative amounts mean refunds, cancellations, adjustments, or returns?
   - Are the amounts all in the same currency?
   - Is the amount tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive?

4. `status`
   - Are there missing statuses?
   - What are the status values?
   - Are statuses updated late?
   - Does finance treat one status as revenue and another as not revenue?

5. `region`, `channel`, `product_category`
   - Are there blank values?
   - Are there inconsistent spellings or codes?
   - Do online and shop values align with channel definitions?

6. `customer_id`
   - Not needed for basic revenue aggregation, but useful if finance reconciles customer invoices or if there are cross-border or bulk customers.

The result of this step should be a list of blocked rows, suspicious rows, and rules for handling them.

### Step 3: Create one canonical weekly revenue table

Build a clean table with one row per order and these fields:

- `order_id`
- `week_start` or `iso_week`
- `region`
- `channel`
- `product_category`
- `amount_raw`
- `amount_revenue_basis`
- `status`
- `include_in_dashboard`
- `exclusion_reason`
- `data_quality_flag`

For each order, apply the agreed rule:

- if it is included, its revenue basis is added to the dashboard;
- if it is excluded, the dashboard does not include it, but it is still recorded with a reason.

Do not silently delete rows. For trust, every excluded order must be visible in the reconciliation.

### Step 4: Aggregate to the dashboard level

Group by:

- week;
- region;
- channel;
- product category.

Measure:

- weekly revenue.

You may also show, on the same dashboard:

- excluded revenue;
- returns or refunds;
- cancelled orders;
- pending unconfirmed orders;
- data quality issues.

But the headline number should be one clearly defined revenue metric.

If the chief executive wants one number, make that number the agreed net recognized revenue. The other numbers should be drill-downs or reconciliation notes, not competing headline metrics.

### Step 5: Build a reconciliation waterfall

This is the key step to stop the “each says the other is wrong” problem.

Start from the raw total amount in the export, then show the differences one by one:

1. Raw total from the export.
2. Minus duplicate or invalid orders.
3. Minus or plus status-based exclusions, such as cancellations, returns, refunds, or pending orders.
4. Minus or plus missing-date or invalid-date adjustments.
5. Minus or plus tax, discount, shipping, or amount-basis adjustments if needed.
6. Minus or plus timing differences between order date and finance recognition date, if finance has a different date.
7. Minus or plus any manual finance adjustments.
8. Equals dashboard revenue.

Then compare that to the finance number and the sales number.

The purpose is not to prove one team right. The purpose is to show the exact reason for the gap.

### Step 6: Validate against finance and sales

Ask each team to check:

- top five weekly totals;
- top five regional totals;
- top five product-category totals;
- top five channel totals;
- the largest excluded orders;
- the largest refunds or cancellations;
- any weeks where sales and finance differ.

A simple validation is:

- Does the dashboard total equal the sum of all included order amounts?
- Does the excluded total plus included total equal the raw eligible total?
- Do the region totals add to the company total?
- Do channel totals add to the company total?
- Do category totals add to the company total?

If the numbers do not tie, the dashboard should not be presented as trusted.

### Step 7: Prepare the Monday meeting answer

For Monday, present the dashboard only if you can answer three questions:

1. What is the revenue rule?
2. Which orders are included and which are excluded?
3. Why does this dashboard differ from the finance or sales view, if it differs?

If finance and sales cannot agree, do not pretend there is one trusted number yet. Instead, present:

- the raw export result;
- the proposed net revenue dashboard under one clear definition;
- a reconciliation table showing the differences;
- a request for a definition sign-off by the end of the day.

That protects the dashboard’s credibility.

## When to stop building

Stop and publish when one of these is true:

1. **Ideal stop**
   - Finance and sales agree on the revenue definition.
   - The data has passed the checks.
   - The dashboard total reconciles to the agreed basis.
   - Any remaining difference is explained and small or accepted.

2. **Practical stop for Monday**
   - You have a clean dashboard based on the best available rule.
   - You have a written reconciliation note.
   - You have flagged any unresolved differences for immediate action.
   - You do not present unresolved ambiguity as a final trusted result.

3. **Stop and delay if**
   - The raw export contains duplicates that cannot be resolved.
   - Finance requires a recognition date that is not present in the file.
   - The `amount` basis is unclear and could materially change revenue.
   - The regional assignment is disputed and the chief executive will use it to judge people.

If a metric will be used to judge managers, an unclear definition is worse than an incomplete dashboard.

## Assumptions I am making

These are assumptions, not facts from your message:

- the discrepancy comes mostly from definition, status handling, timing, or amount basis, not from the data being completely different;
- the export has order IDs that should represent unique orders;
- `amount` is a monetary amount in the same currency;
- the file does not currently include a separate finance posting date, delivery date, invoice date, or payment date;
- the dashboard can use `order_date` as the weekly grouping date, provided this is clearly stated;
- the chief executive’s “one trusted dashboard” requires one headline metric, not a debate over multiple metrics;
- the Monday deadline is tight, so the most important deliverable is a clear rule and reconciliation, not a complex analytics model.

## What I would do first this morning

Before any dashboard is built, send this short request to finance and the sales director:

> For the weekly revenue dashboard, please confirm the following by a fixed time today:  
> 1. Which order statuses count as revenue?  
> 2. Are cancelled, returned, refunded, or pending orders included or excluded?  
> 3. Is `amount` tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive?  
> 4. Does it include discounts, shipping, and adjustments?  
> 5. Is the weekly grouping date `order_date`, or does finance require a recognition date?  
> 6. Does `region` mean sales region, shop region, delivery region, or finance reporting region?  
> 7. How should duplicate or amended order IDs be handled?

Then build from the answer. If there is no answer, build the dashboard under one clearly labelled provisional rule and present it with the reconciliation caveat.

I am the commercial director of a building-materials distributor. Last year we bought a competitor, so we now have two customer lists: about 4,000 accounts in our system and 2,500 in theirs. I want a customer lifetime value model on the combined list so we know which accounts deserve a key-account manager; we can afford one for about 150 accounts. Each system has its own account numbers. Company names were typed by hand, the same contractor often has a separate account for each building site or branch, and many firms bought from both of us. Both systems hold three years of invoices with the account number, date and amount. Nothing is exported yet. My sales reps say the big customers are obvious and the list should find the ones they miss.

## What the problem is

The real decision is: **how to spend scarce key-account-management capacity so it goes to the customers most worth managing in the future**. You have about **4,000 accounts** in your system and about **2,500 accounts** in the acquired competitor’s system, and you can afford a key-account manager for about **150 accounts**.

The result will be used by you, your sales leadership, finance, and the reps who own relationships. It should guide who gets personal management attention, who stays on a lighter-touch route, and which “small” accounts may actually be important.

The unit is not automatically an account number. An account number is only a record in one system. The customer may be:

- one legal company,
- one trading group,
- one contractor with several site or branch accounts,
- one relationship split across your old system and the acquired system,
- or several related accounts that should be managed as one customer.

The moment is now: you are allocating scarce attention before the next commercial cycle, using the past history available in the systems.

### What you told me is known

You know, from your systems:

- account numbers within each system,
- invoice dates,
- invoice amounts,
- three years of history,
- company names typed by hand,
- that the same contractor may have separate accounts for sites or branches,
- that many firms bought from both businesses,
- that reps believe big customers are obvious and the model should find misses,
- that capacity is about 150 accounts.

### What is not known from your description

Important unknowns include:

- whether the 150 slots should be filled by raw accounts or by customer relationships;
- whether invoice amount means gross revenue, net revenue, tax-inclusive billing, or something else;
- whether credits, returns, rebates, and discounts are included or separate;
- customer profitability, gross margin, payment behaviour, credit risk, and cost to serve;
- product mix, region, construction project pipeline, or strategic growth potential;
- whether accounts from the two systems can be matched reliably using names alone;
- whether the same company should be counted as one customer or several site-level customers;
- which reps already cover which accounts;
- whether the acquired customer base is fully comparable to your original customer base.

So the first point is: **a true customer lifetime value model is not possible from invoice date and amount alone**, because lifetime value normally needs future revenue or profit, retention, cost to serve, and margin. What is possible is a strong **value-ranking model based on historical revenue, recent activity, stability, growth, and likely customer identity**.

---

## Possible approaches

### 1. Do no model and rely on reps and managers

This means asking reps to nominate the obvious customers, then reviewing with finance.

**Cost:** very low and quick.  
**What it gives:** a shortlist based on experience and current relationships.  
**What it misses:** customers that reps do not personally know, fragmented customers whose accounts look small individually but large together, fast-growing accounts, and accounts inherited from the acquired business.  
**Useful when:** the customer base is small, well known, and stable. Here it is not enough, because reps have already said they want something that finds accounts they miss.

---

### 2. Rank raw accounts by historical revenue

This means summing invoice amounts for each account, perhaps weighting recent invoices more heavily, and taking the top accounts.

**Cost:** low to medium. Needs data export and simple calculations.  
**What it gives:** an immediate list of high-revenue accounts.  
**What it misses:** customer identity. A contractor with five site accounts may appear lower than they should. A firm buying from both old and new systems may be split across separate records. Also, total revenue alone favours long-standing customers and may miss growing but currently smaller accounts.  
**Useful when:** account numbers are mostly true customers and revenue alone is the main decision criterion. Here it is risky because you already know the same contractor often has multiple accounts and many firms bought from both systems.

---

### 3. Build an entity-resolved historical value model

This is the most practical next step. First try to identify which accounts belong to the same real customer or customer group. Then rank those groups using revenue, recency, consistency, growth, and breadth.

**Cost:** medium. Needs invoice export, name cleanup, some matching rules, and manual review of doubtful merges.  
**What it gives:** a more honest list of “customers” rather than raw records. It can find customers missed by reps because their value is hidden across several accounts, branches, sites, or systems.  
**What it still misses:** profit, strategic value, future growth drivers, and true customer lifetime value unless those can be added later.  
**Why it fits your situation:** your main problem is identity and fragmentation, not a shortage of revenue history.

---

### 4. Build a predictive customer lifetime value model

This would forecast future revenue or profit and then rank customers by expected lifetime value.

**Cost:** higher. Needs customer identity, profit margins, retention, product mix, credit terms, service cost, future pipeline or repeat-purchase labels, and a way to validate the model.  
**What it gives:** a forecast-based ranking, possibly more forward-looking.  
**What it risks:** false precision. With only account number, date, and amount, and without confirmed customer identity, a “lifetime value” model may be estimating a number that the data cannot support.  
**Useful when:** the first model is working but you need better forward-looking decisions, or when finance can provide margin, repeat-purchase, and cost-to-serve data.

---

### 5. Add a selection step for the final 150

Once you have ranked customers or accounts, you may still need to consider balance: coverage, geography, sales-team feasibility, sector mix, growth potential, and whether some accounts should be managed together.

**Cost:** low to medium.  
**What it gives:** a final assignment list that is not just highest value, but workable.  
**Useful when:** the top-ranked list is concentrated in a way that creates practical problems, such as too many accounts under one relationship, too few in some regions, or too many fragmented site accounts.

---

## Recommended approach

I would start with **approach 3: an entity-resolved historical value model**. I would not jump straight to a full predictive lifetime value model yet, because the data you described is not sufficient for profit-based or future-retention-based lifetime value. The model should be treated as a **customer value proxy**, not as an exact lifetime value calculation.

The reason is simple: the biggest risk in your combined base is not that you cannot measure revenue. It is that the revenue may be hidden across account numbers, branches, sites, and systems. A rep may miss a customer because that customer appears as several small accounts rather than one large one. A finance person may miss it because the old competitor’s customers are not comparable to your own. Therefore the first job is to decide what a “customer” is before ranking it.

---

## The plan

### Step 1: Decide what the model must rank

Before any data work, you and your commercial leadership must decide the unit:

- Should the top 150 be **raw account numbers**?
- Should they be **customer relationships**?
- Should branches or sites count separately?
- If one contractor has several accounts, does one key-account manager manage the whole contractor or each site separately?
- Should accounts inherited from the competitor be allowed to compete for slots with your original accounts?

**Assumption if you do not give further instruction:** the business wants to manage customer relationships, but capacity is described in terms of accounts. Therefore the model should produce both:
1. a list of **likely customer groups**, and  
2. a list of **individual accounts** that belong to those groups.

You can then decide whether the 150 slots apply to groups, accounts, or a mixed assignment.

---

### Step 2: Export the data

You need a simple export from both systems:

- account number,
- company name as recorded,
- invoice date,
- invoice amount,
- any address, contact, site, branch, store, region, sales representative, or cost-centre fields available,
- customer master information, if it exists,
- credit memos, returns, discounts, or negative amounts, if stored separately.

**Assumption:** the invoice table contains account number, date, and amount, as you said. Any additional fields are useful but not required to start.

The export should be kept account-level. Do not merge anything at this stage. You need the original account records so you can see which accounts were combined later.

---

### Step 3: Clean the names and account identifiers

Because company names were typed by hand, you need to normalise them before trying to match accounts.

This includes:

- removing extra spaces,
- making case consistent,
- removing punctuation where appropriate,
- standardising common legal words if they do not change the meaning,
- preserving distinct site or branch labels,
- checking whether the name contains words like site, branch, store, depot, project, or location.

**Assumption:** name fields are usable enough to create probable matches, but they will not be perfect.

If each system has its own account number format, the account number cannot be used alone to match customers across systems. It must stay within its original system as a key.

---

### Step 4: Create probable customer groups

Use the cleaned names and any available address, region, site, contact, or master-data fields to group accounts that likely belong to the same customer.

There are two kinds of relationships to look for:

1. **Same customer inside one system**  
   A contractor may have separate accounts for each building site or branch.

2. **Same customer across your system and the acquired system**  
   A firm may have bought from both of you.

You should not merge automatically based only on name similarity. Instead, create a “candidate group” and flag confidence:

- high confidence: exact or near-exact name plus address or site identifiers,
- medium confidence: similar names but no supporting identifier,
- low confidence: similar names that could easily be different firms.

The commercial and sales teams should review the high-value candidate merges. Finance should check anything that would materially change the ranking.

**Assumption:** you have time for human review of doubtful matches. Without human review, fuzzy name matching will create errors that can distort the final list.

---

### Step 5: Build the value metrics

For each unit that will be ranked — account or customer group — calculate metrics from the invoice history. Since you have account number, date, and amount, you can build a practical set:

- **total revenue** over the available history,
- **recent revenue** over the most recent portion of history,
- **earlier revenue** over the prior portion,
- **growth**: recent compared with earlier,
- **recency**: how close the most recent invoice is to now,
- **activity pattern**: how many invoices, and whether revenue appears steady or lumpy,
- **volatility**: whether revenue depends on a single large order or repeat buying,
- **breadth**: whether the customer buys from both systems or across several accounts,
- **size contribution**: share of total revenue in the combined base.

**Assumption:** invoice amount is being treated as a revenue proxy, not as profit. If finance can later provide margin, the model should switch from revenue to contribution margin.

---

### Step 6: Score the units

Use a transparent score, not a complicated prediction model. The score should reflect what you care about:

- current value,
- recent momentum,
- stability,
- future potential as indicated by growing repeat buying,
- and whether the customer is a whole relationship rather than one isolated account.

A sensible starting design is:

- high weight on recent revenue,
- high weight on lifetime revenue,
- meaningful weight on growth,
- meaningful weight on consistency,
- lower weight on single large orders that do not repeat,
- penalty for accounts that look inactive,
- adjustment for known duplicate or fragmented accounts.

The weights should be chosen by you, not hidden inside a black box. You are the commercial director; the model should support your judgment, not replace it.

**Assumption:** you want a ranking method that can be explained to reps and finance. If it cannot be explained, it will be trusted less and used less.

---

### Step 7: Create the shortlist

Produce a ranked list of about **150** recommended customers or accounts, depending on the unit you chose.

Alongside each recommended entry, show:

- the account number or group of accounts,
- the cleaned customer name,
- the original systems involved,
- the revenue figures,
- the recent growth,
- the number of transactions,
- the last invoice date,
- the confidence of the customer merge,
- and the reason the customer is recommended.

Then create two comparison lists:

1. **Reps’ obvious list** — what the sales reps already believe should be key accounts.
2. **Model’s missed list** — accounts or groups that the reps did not nominate but the data suggests are valuable.

This comparison is very important because your reps expect the model to find misses. The output should make that visible.

---

### Step 8: Validate the result

Check the model in three ways.

#### Business validation

Ask the reps and managers to review:

- why a big-looking account is not in the top,
- why a small-looking account or group is in the top,
- whether any merged groups are wrong,
- whether any site accounts should be treated separately,
- whether the top list is practically manageable.

#### Data validation

Use a time split where possible:

- score the accounts using the earlier part of the history,
- check whether that ranking predicts revenue in the recent part,
- look for customers whose value changed materially and understand why.

This tells you whether the historical ranking is useful for looking forward, or whether it is mostly a retrospective revenue list.

#### Sensitivity validation

Check whether the top list changes a lot if you:

- weight recent revenue more,
- weight growth more,
- merge or unmerge doubtful customer groups,
- treat accounts individually rather than grouped,
- change the normalisation method.

If the final list changes dramatically from small adjustments, the model is too dependent on subjective choices. In that case, you need better data or clearer business rules, not a more complicated model.

---

### Step 9: Decide whether to add a real lifetime-value model

Only move from historical ranking to predictive lifetime value if you can add the missing pieces:

- confirmed customer identity,
- profit margins,
- cost to serve,
- credit terms and payment behaviour,
- repeat-purchase behaviour,
- product or service mix,
- churn or retention indicators,
- future pipeline or contract evidence,
- and a way to test whether predicted lifetime value actually matches later customer outcomes.

If those are available later, a predictive model can help refine the shortlist. But if they are not available now, do not pretend a precise lifetime value is possible from invoice amount alone.

---

### Step 10: When to stop

Stop when all of these are true:

- the definition of a customer is agreed;
- high-value customer merges have been reviewed by people who know the accounts;
- the top list is stable under small changes in scoring weights;
- reps and finance accept that the list is reasonable for its purpose;
- the model produces a clear list of missed opportunities, not just the obvious accounts;
- any uncertain accounts are flagged rather than forced into the top or bottom.

Pause, do not force the model further, if:

- the customer identity is too weak to merge safely;
- invoice amounts are not reliable as revenue;
- profit or margin is actually required for the decision but unavailable;
- too many top slots depend on unresolved duplicate accounts;
- reps reject the model’s logic because it cannot be explained.

---

### Facts you gave

### Assumptions in my recommended plan

I am the revenue manager of a travel agency that sells in the UAE and, since last year, to customers in Europe through our website. Cancellations cost us a lot, so I plan to ask for a non-refundable deposit from the bookings most likely to be cancelled and keep the normal terms for everyone else. Please build the model that decides who must pay the deposit. The table I shared has one row per booking: booking date, travel date, destination, the customer's nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether free cancellation was offered, and whether the booking was cancelled. From what I have seen in our reports, nationality tells the most about who cancels, so I expect it to be the main input. The website would apply the rule automatically at checkout. [shares bookings.csv]

You are asking for more than a cancellation forecast. You are asking for a checkout policy: for each website booking, decide whether to require a non-refundable deposit or keep standard cancellation terms. With only the column names and no values, I can design and validate the model and policy, but I cannot fit a usable model yet or set the exact cutoff that decides who pays the deposit.

## What the problem is

The real decision is: **which booking requests should be treated as high-risk and required to pay a non-refundable deposit?**

- **Decision user:** the checkout engine on the website, plus you as revenue manager, finance, and legal for policy setting.
- **Unit of decision:** a single booking request made through the website.
- **Moment of decision:** before the customer completes payment or confirms the booking.
- **Result used:** a risk score or deposit/standard-terms choice shown at checkout.
- **Known information at that moment:** booking date, travel date, destination, channel, lead time, price, whether free cancellation was historically offered, and possibly nationality.
- **Historical outcome available:** whether the past booking was cancelled.
- **Unknown and critical:** how much a cancellation actually costs, how much deposit recovers, how much profit is lost when a customer refuses to book because of a deposit, whether charging a deposit changes behaviour, which variables are legally allowed to affect checkout terms, and the tolerance for false positives.

Your reports suggest nationality is the main signal. I would not build the automated deposit rule around nationality. Using nationality directly in checkout can create legal, fairness, and customer-trust problems, especially for European customers. It can also be a proxy for other booking characteristics such as destination, price, channel, or lead time. Nationality may be useful for diagnosis after the fact, but it should not be the main automated trigger for charging a deposit unless there is a clear, lawful reason such as visa, regulatory, or documented travel-risk rules, not simply “customers from this nationality cancel more.”

Another important limitation: the table lets us predict **who cancelled under past terms**, not necessarily who would cancel if asked to pay a deposit. A deposit may reduce cancellations, but it may also make some customers not book. So the model should be a screening device, and the final policy should be tested before it is rolled out broadly.

## What you told me versus what I assume

**You told me:**
- Cancellations are costly.
- You want to ask high-risk bookings for a non-refundable deposit.
- The decision will be applied automatically at checkout.
- Nationality appears to be the strongest historical signal in your reports.
- The historical table has booking features and a cancellation flag.

- The cancellation flag means the booking was cancelled in a way that caused cost to you.

## Possible approaches, their costs, and what they give

### No model at all: simple business rules
Create deposit rules from obvious booking features, such as long lead time, certain destinations, certain price ranges, certain channels, or past observed high-risk segments.

- **Cost:** lowest effort; can be built from summaries and existing reports.
- **What it gives:** a transparent, easy-to-explain policy; fast to implement; good baseline and fallback.
- **Limits:** it may overcharge too many safe customers or miss risky combinations; it does not produce a proper risk ranking; it cannot answer whether the deposit requirement actually changes behaviour.

### Regularized logistic regression as the first model
Estimate the probability that a booking will be cancelled under historical terms, using booking features such as lead time, destination, price, channel, and whether free cancellation was offered. Nationality would be excluded from the automated decision and checked only separately.

- **Cost:** moderate; needs careful preparation, regularization, validation, and probability calibration.
- **What it gives:** a cancellation-risk probability for each booking; reasonably interpretable; easier to audit than a black-box model; works well when historical data is limited or categories are unstable.
- **Limits:** may miss complex interactions; depends on historical terms; does not prove the effect of changing the deposit policy.

### Flexible machine model, such as boosted trees
Train a more complex model that can discover non-linear patterns and interactions between destination, price, lead time, channel, and seasonality.

- **Cost:** higher effort; needs more careful monitoring, calibration, and explanation; may overfit if the historical sample is limited or time periods differ.
- **What it gives:** potentially stronger risk ranking and better performance on complex patterns.
- **Limits:** harder to justify at checkout; may rely on unfair proxies; more maintenance; probabilities may need extra calibration.

### Cost-based policy model
Use a cancellation-risk score together with business costs: expected cancellation cost, deposit recovery, lost booking margin, and customer lifetime value. The goal becomes choosing the deposit cutoff that maximizes net revenue, not simply predicting cancellations.

- **Cost:** high, because you need financial inputs and possibly experiments.
- **What it gives:** a commercially meaningful rule: charge a deposit only where expected savings exceed expected lost bookings and friction.
- **Limits:** cannot be finalized without costs and testing; a pure prediction model alone is not enough.

### Uplift or randomized policy experiment
Test whether requiring a deposit actually changes outcomes. Give one comparable group standard terms and another a deposit requirement, then compare cancellations, bookings, revenue, and margin.

- **Cost:** highest effort and needs legal, pricing, and customer-experience approval.
- **What it gives:** the most reliable answer to the real business question: who should be charged a deposit under the new policy.
- **Limits:** cannot be done from the historical table alone; requires live testing.

## Chosen approach

I would choose a staged approach:

1. **Start with simple rules as a baseline.**
2. **Build a regularized logistic model to estimate cancellation risk under historical terms.**
3. **Convert risk scores into deposit tiers using cost assumptions.**
4. **Run a controlled checkout experiment before broad rollout.**
5. **Upgrade to a more flexible model only if the logistic model is too weak and the data support it.**

This keeps the first version transparent, auditable, and legally safer, while still improving over manual rules.

## Plan

### Define the target and decision window
Use the cancellation flag as the target for the first model, but confirm whether it includes no-shows, refunds, or only formal cancellations. The model must use only information available at checkout. Booking identifiers and customer identifiers are not features unless you create approved historical features such as prior cancellations or booking frequency.

What you need:
- A clear definition of cancellation cost.
- A confirmation that the target flag matches the costly event you want to prevent or recover.
- Confirmation that price and free-cancellation terms are known at checkout.

### Inspect the historical data
Before modeling, check:
- Whether cancellation is rare or common in each group.
- Missing values.
- Whether price is truly numeric or a coded category.
- Whether destination, nationality, and channel have many rare categories.
- Whether lead time is always available and correctly calculated.
- Whether free cancellation reflects the old terms that your new deposit policy will change.
- Whether website bookings differ from agency bookings.
- Whether older data is still relevant for current customer behaviour.

### Set a no-model baseline
Group bookings by meaningful segments such as channel, destination, lead-time band, price band, and whether free cancellation was offered. Calculate historical cancellation behaviour for those segments. Use this as the fallback rule and benchmark.

If the model cannot beat this baseline on recent data, you should not replace the baseline with a complex model.

### Prepare features without making nationality the automated trigger
For the first production model, exclude nationality from the automated decision. Instead, use features that are operationally available and explainable:
- Lead time.
- Destination, possibly grouped by travel season or risk category.
- Price or price band.
- Channel.
- Whether free cancellation was available historically, used cautiously.
- Booking month or travel season.
- If legally and privacy-approved, customer booking history.

Use nationality separately for validation and monitoring:
- Do high predicted-risk groups contain too many customers from one nationality?
- Is another feature acting as a proxy for nationality?
- Is the deposit rule causing unfair outcomes in protected markets?

### Fit a regularized logistic model
Train a model that outputs a cancellation probability. Use regularization to reduce overfitting, especially because there are categorical fields and a limited historical table.

Important check:
- Split the data by time, not randomly. Train on older bookings, test on newer bookings, and finally validate on the most recent period. Random splits can overstate performance because bookings from the same period leak into training and test.

If the website will apply the rule, also check performance separately on website-like bookings. Offline agency bookings may behave differently.

### Check ranking, calibration, and segment behaviour
Evaluate the model in three ways.

First, check whether it ranks risk correctly:
- Do bookings assigned higher predicted risk actually cancel more often than bookings assigned lower predicted risk?

Second, check calibration:
- If the model assigns similar predicted risk to a group, does the observed cancellation rate in that group match the predicted level?
This matters because the deposit decision depends on the probability level, not only the ranking.

Third, check stability and fairness:
- Does the model behave consistently across time periods?
- Does it create suspicious risk differences by nationality, destination, or channel?
- Can any high-risk decision be explained by business-reasonable features such as lead time, price, destination, and past cancellation history?

### Compare with the baseline
Measure:
- How many cancellations the rule would have flagged in historical data.
- How many likely cancellers it missed.
- How many safe bookings it would have unnecessarily charged.
- Whether the risk tiers are stable.
- Whether it is fairer or at least no worse than simple rules.

### Turn the model into a business cutoff
A cutoff depends on costs, which you have not provided. In plain terms:
- If deposits recover most of the cancellation cost, you can be more aggressive in requesting deposits.
- If many customers abandon checkout when asked for deposits, you should be more selective.
- If only a small share of bookings are truly high-risk, apply deposits to the highest predicted-risk group only.
- If costs are unknown, start with a conservative cutoff and test it.

Use tiers rather than a single harsh boundary if possible:
- Very high predicted risk: deposit required.
- Medium risk: pilot deposit or refundable deposit.
- Low risk: standard terms.

You did not provide deposit amount, cancellation cost, booking margin, or abandonment effect, so I cannot recommend a concrete cutoff.

### Run a controlled checkout experiment
This is the most important step. The model predicts who cancelled historically, but the deposit policy changes behaviour.

Test on comparable bookings:
- Show one group standard terms.
- Show another group the model-driven deposit requirement.
- Compare booking completion, cancellation cost, deposit recovery, margin, and customer experience.

This tells you whether the deposit rule actually saves money or simply deters bookings.

### Deploy with monitoring
If you deploy:
- Apply the rule automatically at checkout.
- Log every decision, input features, predicted risk, final terms, and outcome.
- Provide a manual override for exceptional cases.
- Do not expose discriminatory reasoning to customers.
- Set periodic review: model drift, fairness, cancellation rate, booking abandonment, and financial impact.

### Stop or roll back when
Stop expanding the model-driven deposit policy if:
- It does not beat simple segment rules on recent bookings.
- Predictions are unstable over time.
- Calibration is poor.
- It creates unfair nationality-linked outcomes.
- A pilot shows that deposits reduce bookings more than they prevent cancellation costs.
- Legal or privacy review blocks the use of any key feature.

Adopt it when:
- The model improves risk ranking over the baseline.
- Predictions are calibrated well enough for tiering.
- The business threshold gives expected net savings.
- The pilot confirms positive outcomes under the new terms.
- Fairness and legal review are passed.

## What I need before the model can be practically finalized

To build and tune the actual policy, you need to provide or confirm:
- Cancellation cost per booking.
- Deposit amount and refund rules.
- Typical booking margin or profit.
- Expected checkout abandonment when a deposit is requested.
- Legal position on using nationality, destination, channel, and customer history.
- Whether customer history is available at checkout.
- Whether no-shows are included in cancellation cost.
- Whether the historical table includes enough website bookings to represent the future rule.
- How much overcharging of safe customers is acceptable.

The most useful first model is not a nationality-driven cancellation predictor. It is a transparent risk-scoring model using checkout-time booking features, combined with a cost-based cutoff and a controlled deposit experiment.

## What the problem really is

### The decision being supported
The business needs to decide which newly placed orders deserve a proactive phone call from customer care before shipping, in order to reduce refunds by confirming product and delivery details.

The core predictive question is:

**Given only what is known when the order is placed, how likely is this order to end in a refund?**

### Who will use the result
The primary user is the customer care team, who will score each new order and contact the buyers with the highest risk.

Secondary users may include operations, finance, and category or regional merchandising, because repeated patterns could later inform pricing, fulfillment, packaging, or product listing quality.

The unit is an **order**.

That means the model must only use information that would actually be available at that instant.

## Approaches that could solve this

### Approach 1: No model at all, just business rules
This would be a list of manual calling rules, such as:
- phone orders in certain regions,
- phone certain channels,
- phone high-value orders,
- phone certain product categories,
- phone new customers or first-time buyers.

**What it costs**
- Very low.
- Easy to explain.
- Can be set up quickly.
- Does not require engineering or maintenance.

**What it gives**
- Simple targeting.
- Useful if refund risk is obvious and concentrated.
- Poor at discovering subtle patterns.
- Likely to either call too many orders or miss risky ones.

This is a good fallback if the data is too small or too unreliable for modeling.

---

### Approach 2: A segment baseline
This would estimate refund risk by simple groups such as:
- refund rate by region,
- refund rate by channel,
- refund rate by product category,
- refund rate by amount band,
- refund rate by customer type, such as new versus repeat.

**What it costs**
- Low to moderate.
- Easy to compute.
- Easy to maintain.

**What it gives**
- A sensible starting probability.
- A benchmark for whether a real model is worth it.
- Some transparency.
- It cannot capture interactions very well, such as “high-value orders in one category but only in one channel.”
- It also cannot learn much about individual customers.

This should absolutely be used as a comparison point.

---

### Approach 3: A regularized logistic regression model
This would be a yes/no refund model using simple, stable features:
- region,
- channel,
- product category,
- order amount,
- time-related order features if available,
- customer history features computed only from past orders.

Regularization means the model is penalized so it does not chase small quirks in limited data.

**What it costs**
- Moderate.
- Requires careful encoding of categorical variables.
- Requires time-aware customer history to avoid leakage.
- Needs validation over time, not just random splits.

**What it gives**
- Usually the best balance here:
  - interpretable,
  - stable,
  - fast to score,
  - good when data is not huge,
  - produces risk scores and probabilities.
- It can reveal which factors actually matter.
- It can be used immediately for ranking orders.

This is a strong primary candidate for your situation.

### Approach 4: A gradient-boosted tree model
This would use decision-tree-style learning to find interactions and non-linear patterns.

**What it costs**
- Higher.
- Needs careful tuning.
- Needs stronger validation because small tables can cause overfitting.
- Needs extra work to explain to non-technical teams.

**What it gives**
- Potentially better ranking than logistic regression if there are real interactions.
- Can handle messy feature scales more naturally.
- May be useful as a challenger model, but usually not the best first choice when the goal is a simple, reliable pre-shipment calling model.

---

### Approach 5: A customer-behavior model
This would emphasize patterns such as:
- how many past orders the customer has placed,
- how many past refunds they have had,
- how recent their last order was,
- whether they are new or repeat,
- their typical order amount.

**What it costs**
- Moderate to high if done properly.
- Must be built very carefully to avoid leakage.
- Needs stable customer identification.

**What it gives**
- Potentially very strong if there are habitual refunders.
- Very useful in retail settings, because past refund behavior can matter a lot.
- If the customer base is mostly one-time buyers, this will help less.

## The approach I would choose

I would choose:

**A time-aware logistic regression model for refund risk, using order features plus leakage-safe customer history features, with a segment baseline as the comparison benchmark.**

Why this one:
- Your export is order-level and likely not huge.
- You need a model that is stable, fast, and easy to defend.
- The business decision is about ranking riskiest orders.
- Logistic regression usually gives good performance with modest data.
- Customer history can add real value if repeat buyers exist.
- It is easier to explain to customer care than a large ensemble model.

## The model plan, step by step

### Step 1: Define the target clearly
**Goal:** Create a clean refund/no-refund label from `status`.

**Needs:**
- The full set of distinct `status` values.
- Business agreement on what counts as a refund.
- A decision on partial refunds:
  - If partial refunds count as refunds for the calling policy, treat them as refund events.
  - If not, define the target accordingly.

**Check:**
- Each order maps to exactly one label.
- The label is final and not contaminated by future information.

**Stop this step when:**
- The refund definition is agreed and reproducible.

---

### Step 2: Confirm what is known at order placement
**Goal:** Avoid features that only exist after the outcome is known.

**Needs:**
- Verification that `amount` is the order amount at placement.
- Verification that `region`, `channel`, and `product_category` are known before shipping.
- Verification of whether `order_date` includes time of day.

**Check:**
- Any field that depends on delivery outcome, customer confirmation, cancellation, or refund processing must be excluded.

**Stop this step when:**
- You have a safe list of pre-placement features.

---

### Step 3: Clean the order table
**Goal:** Make the export reliable enough for modeling.

**Needs:**
- Duplicate order ID check.
- Missing values review.
- Date ordering check.
- Amount plausibility check.
- Status consistency check.

**Check:**
- Each order is represented once.
- Outcomes make sense.
- Date fields are correctly ordered.
- No impossible values appear.

**Stop this step when:**
- You know how many rows will be used and how missing values are handled.

---

### Step 4: Split the data by time
This is critical.

Because the model will score orders as they arrive, you should not randomly shuffle the rows. You should simulate the real deployment situation.

**Goal:** Train on older orders and test on newer orders.

**Needs:**
- Valid order dates.
- A time-based split.
- Ideally several rolling-origin checks rather than a single lucky split.

**Check:**
- Recent-period orders are never used to predict older orders.
- Validation is based on the kind of data the model would face in production.

**Stop this step when:**
- You have a time-based evaluation design that reflects live scoring.

---

### Step 5: Build features from order characteristics
These are the stable, simple predictors:
- region,
- channel,
- product category,
- amount,
- time-related features if available.

For categorical fields:
- use one-hot encoding for categories with manageable counts;
- merge very rare categories into an “Other” type if needed, based only on training data;
- avoid letting the model memorize tiny patterns from rare labels.

For amount:
- if it is very skewed, use a transformation such as a logarithmic or rank-style transformation.

**Needs:**
- Training-only decisions on rare category handling.
- Stable encoding logic that can be reused on new orders.

**Check:**
- Feature transformations are computed only from training data.
- Scoring logic is reproducible on future orders.

**Stop this step when:**
- The feature set is stable enough to be reproduced in production.

---

### Step 6: Build leakage-safe customer history features
This is often where the real signal is.

Possible history features include:
- number of previous orders by this customer before the current order,
- number of previous refunds before the current order,
- refund rate on past orders before the current order,
- days since previous order,
- average previous order amount,
- whether the current order is the customer’s first order.

**Needs:**
- A time-aware history table.
- For each order, features must use only customer events strictly before that order.
- A rule for missing history for first-time customers.

**Check:**
- No current-order outcome is ever used in customer history.
- No future order by the same customer is ever used.
- First-time customers are handled explicitly, not treated as random missing data.

**Stop this step when:**
- Customer history features are reproducible exactly the same way on new orders.

---

### Step 7: Compare a simple baseline before modeling
Before fitting a model, compare with:
- a constant average refund rate,
- segment-level refund rates,
- maybe a very simple rules-based calling policy.

**Needs:**
- The baseline predictions on the same time-based validation data.

**Check:**
- The model must do better than the baseline in ranking orders, not just in raw accuracy.

**Stop this step when:**
- You know whether modeling is likely to add real value.

---

### Step 8: Train the logistic regression model
**Goal:** Learn a score that orders risky refunds above safe ones.

**Needs:**
- Time-based training split.
- Regularized model to control overfitting.
- Handling of imbalance if refund orders are much rarer than non-refunds.

**Check:**
- Training is done only on earlier orders.
- Regularization strength is chosen from validation data, not final test data.
- Feature coefficients are sensible enough to review.

**Stop this step when:**
- The model trains stably and does not swing wildly with small data changes.

---

### Step 9: Evaluate the model the way the business needs it
Because customer care is calling the riskiest orders, the most important evaluation is not plain accuracy.

You should check:

#### Ranking quality
Does the model put refund orders near the top and safe orders near the bottom?

#### Top-risk capture
Among the orders that would be called under the current capacity, how many would actually have refunded?

This is often the most relevant measure.

#### Calibration
When the model says the average risk in a score group is a certain level, does that match the observed refund rate in that group?

#### Stability over time
Does the model’s usefulness hold across multiple later order windows, not just one lucky test period?

#### Explainability
Can customer care and merchandising understand which factors are driving risk?

**Needs:**
- Final time-based test.
- Clear comparison with baseline and rules.
- Review by the team that will actually act on the scores.

**Stop this step when:**
- The model clearly improves on the baseline for the calling use case.

---

### Step 10: Decide what “risky enough to call” means
Because you did not give call costs, refund costs, or team capacity, I will not invent a threshold.

Instead, the cutoff should be set by business logic:

- If customer care can call a certain number of orders, score all orders, rank them, and flag the highest-risk ones up to that capacity.
- If you know the expected savings from preventing a refund and the cost of a call, set the threshold where expected benefit turns positive.

**Needs:**
- Refund cost.
- Saving from a prevented refund.
- Call handling cost.
- Capacity of the customer care team.

**Check:**
- The chosen cutoff actually matches what the team can do without flooding them.

**Stop this step when:**
- The action threshold is operationally realistic and tied to cost or capacity, not a made-up score value.

---

### Step 11: Build the scoring pipeline for new orders
**Goal:** Score each new order as it comes in.

**Needs:**
- Same feature definitions used in training.
- Same rare-category handling.
- Same amount transformation.
- Same customer history calculation.
- A way to handle first-time customers.

**Check:**
- The exact same code or logic can be used for training and scoring.
- A new order gets a score without needing future data.

**Stop this step when:**
- You can reproduce historical training features from current inputs without leakage.

---

### Step 12: Monitor the model after launch
**Goal:** Make sure it stays useful.

**Needs:**
- Actual refund outcomes for scored orders.
- Score distributions over time.
- Feature drift monitoring for region, channel, category, and amount patterns.
- Customer care feedback on whether flagged orders are genuinely risky.

**Check:**
- Are high-risk scores still mostly refund orders?
- Is the model still beating the baseline?
- Are new categories or channels behaving differently?

**Stop this step when:**
- You have a clear rule for when to retrain:
  - if capture of refund orders drops noticeably,
  - if score distributions change sharply,
  - if business categories or channels shift,
  - or if customer behavior changes materially.

---

## When to stop the whole modeling effort and use something simpler
I would stop modeling and rely on a baseline or rules-based policy if:

- refund positives are too sparse for any stable pattern to be learned;
- the model does not beat the segment baseline on recent orders;
- feature definitions are not reliable enough for live scoring;
- the call threshold cannot be justified without better cost data;
- most refunds are driven by factors not in this table.

In that case, the best next step is not a fancier model, but better data collection.

---

## What I would want to collect to make this stronger
The current table is enough to start, but it is not enough to know the full cause of refund risk.

To improve the model, you should also capture:
- delivery address risk signals,
- customer tenure or lifecycle stage,
- product item details,
- price band and shipping option,
- order item count,
- refund reason code,
- whether the customer contacted care before refunding,
- whether delivery was modified before shipment,
- whether the order was fulfilled on time,
- and whether there are repeat cancellations or failed deliveries.

Without these, the model may predict who is likely to refund, but not why.

---

Build a **time-based, leakage-safe logistic regression model** that scores each order at placement using:
- order region,
- channel,
- product category,
- amount,
- and past customer behavior up to that order date.

Use a **segment baseline** as the comparison benchmark, and choose the calling threshold by **customer care capacity and expected refund savings**, not by an arbitrary score cutoff. If the model does not beat the baseline on recent held-out orders, fall back to simple calling rules and improve the data before trying a more complex model.
